node.label: E. A. Wrigley
node.date_label: Cambridge Group founded (with Laslett) 1964 · with Schofield, The Population History of England 1981 · Ellen McArthur lectures 1987 · Continuity, Chance and Change 1988 · with Davies, Oeppen and Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution 1997 · Poverty, Progress, and Population 2004 · Energy and the English Industrial Revolution 2010 · The Path to Sustained Growth 2016
node.description: A historical demographer and economic historian at Cambridge, who founded the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure with Peter Laslett in 1964. With Roger Schofield he reconstructed England’s population from the registers of 404 parishes by “back projection”, making it “possible for the first time” to follow “a secular cycle of population development” and its relation to economic change (1981); a family-reconstitution study, a technique perfected by Louis Henry, was its complement (1997). He called the industrial revolution his “first main research interest”, to which he “returned increasingly” after years of population history. In Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), from his 1987 Ellen McArthur lectures, he questioned it as “a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon”: growth came from two sets of forces with “only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time”, as an “organic economy” bounded by the productivity of the land met a new one using mineral energy. Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010) asked “not how the period of more rapid growth began, but why it did not come to an end”, without offering energy as the only explanation: there could be “no single, ‘true’ account”, and to downplay institutional and scientific explanations would be “presumptuous and mildly ridiculous”. Mining coal “provided the solution” (2016). He judged Rostow’s “take-off” “now almost impossible to maintain” (2004). Berg and Hudson questioned causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s aggregate studies (1990). Readers set his energy argument beside Pomeranz’s coal (Mokyr in a draft of 2002, Huang in 2002, Clark and Jacks in 2007), and Wong said that China Transformed had followed his arguments on coal (2016).
node.representative_figures_and_works: E. A. (Tony) Wrigley (1931–2022); with R. S. Schofield, The Population History of England, 1541–1871: A Reconstruction (1981); People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change: The Character of the Industrial Revolution in England (1988); with R. S. Davies, J. E. Oeppen and R. S. Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution, 1580–1837 (1997); Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004); Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010); “Energy and the English Industrial Revolution” (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 2013); The Path to Sustained Growth (2016). Co-founder, with Peter Laslett, of the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (1964). Readers and critics: Maxine Berg and Pat Hudson (1990); Joel Mokyr and Philip Huang (2002); Gregory Clark and David Jacks (2007); R. Bin Wong (2016).
node.scope_note: Read in Cambridge University Press excerpts: The Population History of England (1981; the introduction of the 1989 paperback, pp. 1–5, OCRed), English Population History from Family Reconstitution (1997, pp. 3–4), Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004, pp. 1–3) and Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11), on 2026-10-18; Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8) and The Path to Sustained Growth (2016, pp. 1–4) in revision 1.145; the 2013 article in abstract only. The Cambridge Group’s founding and projects come from its institutional history. The rest of each book is unread, including the statistical reconstruction, and no estimate is adjudicated; Berg and Hudson’s objection concerns causal inference from the aggregate studies, not the reconstruction as such; the reconstruction and the reconstitution volume were collaborative, with Schofield, Oeppen and Davies. People, Cities and Wealth (1987) is unread. The comparisons with Pomeranz are readers’: no passage in which Pomeranz acknowledges Wrigley’s energy argument was read. Wong’s statement that China Transformed followed Wrigley is his 2016 retrospective. The wider argument about why industrialisation happened in Britain is held by the debate entry capitalismdebates; his population work stays on demography/aggregate_population.

incident_edges.relationship: The Industrial Revolution as escape from an “organic economy” bounded by land: growth from two sets of forces with “only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time” (1988), the question “why it did not come to an end”, without dismissing institutional or scientific explanations (2010), and coal as “the solution” (2016); Berg and Hudson questioned causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s aggregate studies (1990)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words, in Cambridge University Press excerpts. Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8 read in revision 1.145): “After many years spent in work principally concerned with the population history of England, I had returned increasingly to my first main research interest, the better understanding of the industrial revolution” (p. 1); “My main aim in the lectures was to question the appropriateness of the view that the industrial revolution was a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon” (p. 3); growth was “the product of two different sets of forces having only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time” (p. 4); the classical economists remain authoritative for “an economy bounded by the productivity of the land, what I shall term an organic economy” (p. 5). Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11 read): “the most important single issue on which to focus in trying to gain a clearer understanding of the industrial revolution is not how the period of more rapid growth began, but why it did not come to an end” (p. 4); “the production horizon for all organic economies was set by the annual cycle of plant growth” (p. 9); “There can be no single, ‘true’ account of the industrial revolution” (p. 4); institutional and scientific explanations get “only glancing references”, but “it would be both presumptuous and mildly ridiculous to downplay their importance”, and the explanations are “essentially incommensurable” (pp. 4–5). The Path to Sustained Growth (2016, p. 3): “Mining coal provided the solution to this problem.” Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004, pp. 1–3): Rostow’s “take-off” is “now almost impossible to maintain” (p. 2), and Berg and Hudson put the counter-view “vigorously and effectively” (p. 3 n. 6). The 2013 article is read in abstract only. Critique: Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper, read): “The work of Wrigley and Schofield dominates the population history of this period and illustrates some of the more general problems of causal analysis based on aggregative studies.” Their objection concerns causal inference from the aggregate series, not the reconstruction as such. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from demography because Wrigley had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to e_a_wrigley and keeps its id. His population reconstruction is drawn on e_a_wrigley → demography.

incident_edges.relationship: Reconstructing England’s population from parish registers: with Schofield, 404 parishes and “back projection” to trace “a secular cycle of population development” and its relation to economic change (1981), complemented by family reconstitution (1997), in the Cambridge Group he co-founded (1964)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Wrigley and Schofield, The Population History of England (1981; introduction pp. 1–5 read in the publisher excerpt of the 1989 Cambridge paperback, OCRed): “since pre-industrial societies normally experienced great difficulty in achieving a rapid expansion in their capacity to produce goods and services, population was the more dynamic element in the striking of a balance with production” (p. 1); the registers make it “possible for the first time to establish with some precision what changes took place in a pre-industrial population over a period of time long enough to encompass a secular cycle of population development, and to investigate the relationship between demographic and economic change during its course” (p. 2); monthly totals “taken from the registers of a total of 404 parishes” (p. 3); “the technique of back projection, which was developed to make the best use of the aggregative data assembled” (p. 4); the aggregative tabulations began as “a subsidiary element” of the Cambridge Group’s family-reconstitution work of “the middle 1960s” (p. 5). Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997, pp. 3–4, read): “This book is intended as a complement to the Population history of England”; family reconstitution “had then recently been perfected by Louis Henry”. The Cambridge Group’s institutional history (read) dates its founding by Laslett and Wrigley to 1964. A collaborative project: Schofield, Oeppen and Davies share these results, and the reconstruction’s estimates are not adjudicated here. Berg and Hudson’s critique of its “aggregative” use for causal analysis is on e_a_wrigley → capitalismdebates (edge_1084).

incident_edges.relationship: Technologies to exploit coal as Europe’s difference: China Transformed (1997) followed “arguments of E. A. Wrigley”, as Wong recalled in 2016
incident_edges.evidence_note: Wong, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 26:3, 2016, p. 76, read): “The cluster of differences stressed in that work concerned European science and technologies, and in particular, following arguments of E. A. Wrigley, the importance of technologies to exploit coal as a source of energy to power new kinds of machines”; his note cites Continuity, Chance and Change (1988). Qualification: this is Wong’s retrospective account. China Transformed is read only in chapter openings, and the passage that cites Wrigley there was not read. Wrigley’s own organic-economy argument is on e_a_wrigley → capitalismdebates (edge_1084).

incident_edges.relationship: Coal in explanations of British industrialisation, as readers compare them: Mokyr places Pomeranz in a tradition “established by … E.A. Wrigley” (2002); Huang says Pomeranz simplified “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument” (2002); Clark and Jacks find that both “have made coal central to the story” (2007)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Readers’ comparisons, read. Mokyr (October 2002 draft, p. 2): Pomeranz’s coal argument “joins a venerable tradition established by Carlo Cipolla, E.A. Wrigley and others that looks at the Industrial Revolution as primarily a revolution of fossil fuel usage”. Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 532–533, read in revision 1.144): Wrigley (1988) is “a very different thing from arguing that chance, or coal, alone mattered”; Pomeranz has turned “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument that chance figured in England’s industrialization into a simple argument that coal and colonies alone mattered.” Clark and Jacks (European Review of Economic History 2007, abstract): “both E. A. Wrigley and Kenneth Pomeranz have made coal central to the story”; their coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England’s possession of coal reserves. A comparison, not an influence: no passage in which Pomeranz acknowledges Wrigley’s energy argument was read (the read pages of The Great Divergence cite Wrigley only on England’s early divergence from the continent, p. 6 n. 8). Wrigley’s argument stresses chance and the end of the organic economy; Pomeranz pairs coal with colonies.

named_group_routes.relationship: De Vries uses demographic research on marriage, mortality, fertility and households to revise accounts of early modern economic change
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. His 1994 article, p. 252, explicitly discusses demographic contributions and cites Henry, Laslett, Hajnal, Wrigley and Schofield among others. This named use strengthens the formerly generic field link. Hajnal’s own primary argument is now checked separately: it includes category/geography limits and economic hypotheses in both causal directions. De Vries’s particular use does not convert these into a proved general mechanism.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Cambridge Group’s finding that the western European nuclear family long predated industrialisation, with Hajnal’s marriage pattern, as one of the literatures that “guided my thinking” (2008)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The Industrious Revolution (2008, p. 8, publisher excerpt, read): among four “modern developments in history and economics” that “have guided my thinking”, “3. The Western European Marriage Pattern. The pioneering work of ‘The Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure’ established the view that the nuclear family structures of modern western European countries and their offshoots are not a product of industrialization but have much earlier origins”, with “the seminal articles of John Hajnal”; “its distinctive economic behavior remains an open question.” The 1994 article’s reference list (Cambridge Core, metadata) cites Wrigley and Schofield (1981), Laslett (1965, 1977) and Hajnal (1965). The influence is credited to the Cambridge Group and Hajnal, not to Wrigley alone; demography/john_hajnal already records Hajnal as a resource for de Vries.

verification.note: University-hosted primary scan downloaded and visually read at pp. 249–252 and 259–264. Supports household labor/resource reallocation, demand, explicit use of historical demography, and qualifications about intrahousehold interests and ideal types. The article criticizes McKendrick’s gendered wording and discusses Sabean’s household critique. No claim that all households followed this trajectory; quantitative estimates and later reception not independently replicated. Addendum 2026-10-18: Pp. 249–251 re-read for revision 1.145 (page images OCRed): the framing against the revision of Lindert and Williamson, Harley and Crafts, and n. 5 citing Berg and Hudson and Cannadine. Addendum 2026-10-18: Revision 1.146 read the publisher abstract and the reference list on Cambridge Core (doi:10.1017/S0022050700014467); the url is the DOI (source_field_sets). The page readings recorded above were made in earlier revisions and were not repeated in 1.146. The new jan_de_vries entry and the revised edge_1085 quote the 1994 article only from its publisher abstract; previously accepted page-based claims remain as accepted.

verification.note: Read OCR of printed501–506 and533–535, including conclusion and weights/measures appendix. Map images504–505 not visually inspected; remaining empirical sections and bibliography536–538 unread. Criticism of labor productivity, household production and coal demand is attributed, not a numerical verdict. First-page JSTOR wrapper incorrectly says Greater; article title says Great. Huang’s1990 book is identified in this exchange and Stanford publisher metadata, but its body is unread.2002 is retrospective criticism of mapped work, not a scope extension. Addendum 2026-10-18: Revision 1.144: the whole article was OCRed (tesseract) from the same JSTOR scan; pp. 501–503, 511–512, 515 and 530–535 read closely, the rest searched. p. 501 thanks "Chris Isett … Robert Brenner"; p. 502: "It is not built on original research, but rather relies on past secondary scholarship"; p. 503: "what I termed in my work development (involving increased labor productivity), to distinguish it from involution (involving diminishing marginal returns per unit of labor) and intensification (added labor input per unit of land) in the Yangzi delta (1990, 11)"; p. 512: "growth (in output) without development (in labor productivity) … the familization of production"; p. 515 cites Geertz 1963 (pp. 130–43) only for Japan; pp. 530–531 tie his Qing law studies ("a survival ethic") to the argument; p. 533: Pomeranz's coal argument "places the cart before the horse", and "Pomeranz, I wish to emphasize, has made a useful contribution"; p. 534: England and the delta "were in fact virtually at opposite poles in a continuum from development to involution". Huang's rejoinder and Pomeranz's second response are in JAS 62:1 (2003), not this issue. The second research pass (evidence-pomeranz.pass2.md §2) OCRed the same scan (all 38 article pages, 200 dpi) and read pp. 501–503, 514–515, 520–521 and 532–534 in full, p. 508 (n. 7) and the reference list pp. 536–538; pp. 520–521: Pomeranz "tries to take the revolution out of de Vries' industrious revolution", and Huang (p. 521) "ignores … the evidence de Vries and others have generated to document the big changes in consumption patterns", as that pass reads it. Both passes OCRed the whole article; each read only the pages listed closely.
